---
title: "Building 'Us' in the Image of 'I': The Constructive Cognitive Architecture of Social Identity"
shorttitle: "Constructive Architecture of Social Identity"
author:
  - name: Jacob J. Elder
    affiliations:
      - name: University of California, Riverside
        department: Psychology
    corresponding: true
    email: jelder@ucr.edu
abstract: |
  People tend to see themselves as similar to their ingroup, often by projecting self-beliefs onto their perceptions of others. The within-person cognitive mechanisms underlying this process remain under-specified. This research formalizes self-anchoring as similarity-based generalization across a semantic trait network, establishing the relational (e.g., if I am outgoing, my group should be characteristic of semantically related traits like sociable) and contrastive (i.e., how the ingroup compares to a specific outgroup) mechanisms through which self-evaluations generalize to the ingroup. Across three studies using minimal groups (N = 61), university groups (N = 181), and racial groups (N = 265), individuals used semantic similarity among traits to infer group characteristics from their own attributes. Self-anchoring was primarily driven by a motivation to achieve similarity with the ingroup. In the racial context, minority participants contrasting against the racial majority were more strongly driven to achieve dissimilarity from the majority outgroup. The projection rate itself remained invariant across intergroup contexts, but the prior ingroup preference (γ) attenuated sharply when participants contrasted against a positively-regarded, higher-status outgroup (Study 2). In Study 3, similarity-based inference was suppressed entirely under minority–minority outgroup contrasts; in the racial context, pre-existing cultural stereotypes compete with self-anchoring, increasing classification noise and limiting generalization. Model-derived semantic contrast ratios (MCR) correlated with social identification, self-esteem, and prototypicality across studies.
keywords: [self-anchoring, social identity, category learning, semantic similarity, computational modeling]
format:
  apaquarto-docx: default
---

## INTRODUCTION
People carry stable self-beliefs across situations (Markus & Wurf, 1987) yet maintain a sense of belonging (Baumeister & Leary, 1995) by assimilating into their social groups (Brewer, 1991; Ellemers et al., 2001). Through this similarity, social identification emerges—a sense of positive attachment central to group life (Tajfel, 1978; Turner et al., 1987). Social psychology has conceptualized group membership as "depersonalization," where the self is categorized as an interchangeable exemplar of a group prototype (Turner et al., 1987). This account—often termed "self-stereotyping"—emphasizes assimilation of group attributes into the self-concept but does not explain how people identify with novel groups or maintain self-beliefs that remain stable across group memberships (van Veelen et al., 2016).

Rather than only assimilating group attributes, people also project their own attributes onto how they represent their ingroups (M. Cadinu & Rothbart, 1996) and others in interpersonal contexts (Ames, 2004). This process, known as self-anchoring, serves as an informational base (Gramzow et al., 2001) from which people draw inferences about their social environment. Individuals engage in inductive reasoning, inferring unknown information about their group from their own self-knowledge (DiDonato et al., 2011; Krueger, 2007). Self-anchoring is most pronounced when group knowledge is ambiguous or diagnostic information is absent (van Veelen et al., 2013a), making it central to the emergence of social identity.

The present approach differs fundamentally from the social projection literature (Krueger, 1998; Ames, 2004; Van Boven & Loewenstein, 2003), which treats self-to-group inference as a Bayesian base-rate problem: one's own trait level adjusts a prior belief about the group mean, with each trait evaluated independently. We model self-anchoring instead as similarity-based generalization across a structured semantic network. This distinction is consequential: it allows us to test whether self-knowledge propagates *through relational structure* to traits the person never directly evaluated—a form of inference that base-rate accounts cannot generate and that directly constitutes generalization in the category learning sense.

### Inferences About the Ingroup Based on the Self
Despite the apparent strength of evidence for self-anchoring, the majority of research in this domain has relied on correlated ratings of identical traits across the self and group (M. Cadinu & Rothbart, 1996; Otten & Wentura, 2001). While these tests provide evidence of rating stability, they do not necessarily demonstrate *generalization* per se. Furthermore, traditional measures are vulnerable to repetition effects; the mere repetition of information can cause it to be perceived as more characteristic (Unkelbach et al., 2019). A rigorous test of the generalization-based theory of self-anchoring requires establishing that self-evaluations generalize across semantically related but novel traits (Heit & Rubinstein, 1994). For example, if an individual perceives themselves as "outgoing," do they infer that their group is characteristic of semantically similar traits like "sociable" and "fun," even if they have not explicitly evaluated themselves on those specific attributes?

In the current research, we move social identity theory from a verbal, descriptive model to a formal architecture by integrating principles of category learning. We frame the self as a semantic prototype in a high-dimensional space, where group beliefs emerge through similarity-based generalization consistent with Shepard's (1987) universal law of generalization. To formalize this process, we utilize a semantic dependency network of 147 positive traits, constructed using data from 178 Amazon Mechanical Turk participants with a 25% consensus threshold. From this network, we derive relational similarity measures (network-based Dice similarity; Equation 1) that allow us to quantify how self-representations propagate across the trait network.

This network approach enables the first formal implementation of the "metacontrast principle," which posits that group categorization is defined by the ratio of an individual’s similarity to the ingroup relative to the individual’s similarity to the outgroup (Turner et al., 1987). While the metacontrast principle has been central to social identity research for decades, it has remained a verbal description (Davis & Goldwater, 2021). Structurally, Turner's metacontrast ratio is formally isomorphic to Nosofsky's (1986) Generalized Context Model—both define category membership via a ratio of summed similarities; we provide the formal backbone Turner's verbal architecture required. By applying a category learning framework to social identity, we provide a formal test of whether intergroup contrast accentuates self-anchoring and how individuals balance the motivation for ingroup similarity against outgroup differentiation.

### Relational Similarity as the Basis for Self-Concept Generalization
Generalizing from known to novel stimuli based on similarity is a core cognitive capacity (Shepard, 1987). In prior work, we developed a semantic network of trait dependencies (J. Elder et al., 2023) to extract relational similarity based on shared semantic neighbors, moving beyond simple trait-for-trait matching. Similarity-based inference drives both classification within categories and contrast of distinctive features between them (Tversky, 1977).

Social identity research has borrowed heavily from cognitive science research on concept learning, yet it has rarely implemented the formalism leveraged by that field. The ability to make representational claims about the role of similarity-based inference in social categorization has previously been limited by the absence of model formalism (Guest & Martin, 2021). Here, we bridge this gap by implementing formal category learning models—such as the Generalized Context Model (Nosofsky, 1986)—to test the principles of social categorization in a self-anchoring context. This formal bridge between Shepard's (1987) universal law of generalization, Nosofsky's GCM, and Turner's metacontrast principle constitutes the paper's central theoretical ambition: to instantiate in a computational model what social identity theory has long claimed in words.

### The Current Design
We utilize a "training-to-generalization" paradigm common in concept learning research (Bowman et al., 2020). Participants first self-evaluate on a subset of traits (training phase), which serve as exemplars of the self-concept prototype. This is followed by a "generalization phase" where participants classify traits—including novel traits not seen during training—as more characteristic of either the ingroup or outgroup. Using the traits’ semantic similarities to the self-concept, we predict the likelihood of ingroup classification.

Across three studies, we examine how various intergroup contexts amplify or attenuate these generalization weights. Study 1 utilizes minimal groups to provide a proof-of-concept for similarity-based generalization. Study 2 examines the role of relative social status using university groups, testing whether status context modulates the prior ingroup preference (γ), the projection rate (α), or the breadth of self-concept generalization (λ)—and whether real social categories with meaningful status histories can dissociate ingroup assimilation from outgroup repulsion in ways that minimal groups cannot. Study 3 applies this framework to racial identities, examining how majority or minority outgroup contrasts exert differential effects on the tendency to self-anchor. This framework operationalizes the "sense of sameness" (James, 1890) underlying group identification.

## STUDY 1: SELF-ANCHORING BASED ON MINIMAL CONDITIONS
Study 1 provided a first proof-of-concept for similarity-based generalization in a minimal group context where group knowledge is absent. Study 1 was pre-registered at OSF (https://osf.io/7jn3e). We pre-registered three predictions: that Similarity-to-Self (SS) predicts ingroup classification, that this effect extends to novel unseen traits, and that individual differences in independent self-construal, self-esteem, need for cognition, and self-concept clarity would correlate with self-anchoring strength. Computational modeling analyses and MCR-based individual differences are exploratory.

### Methods
**Participants**
From an initial pool of 80 participants, 19 were excluded (final *N* = 61). Exclusions were applied for: failure to consent to data use after debriefing (*n* = 9), self-reported low task seriousness (< 4 on a 7-point item; *n* = 1), self-reported unusable data (*n* = 2), and careless responding — defined as > 80% identical self-evaluations, > 95% identical group classifications, or > 40% missing responses in either phase (*n* = 10). Participants were native English-speaking university students (40.98% Cisgender Female, 59.02% Cisgender Male; *M*<sub>Age</sub> = 19.95, *SD*<sub>Age</sub> = 1.51, Range<sub>Age</sub> = [18, 25]), with an ethnic composition of 9.84% White/Caucasian, 11.48% Mixed/Other, 32.79% Asian, 40.98% Hispanic/Latino, and 4.92% Native-American. A power analysis using *simr* (Green & MacLeod, 2016) on a prior relational similarity dataset indicated that *N* = 5 was sufficient to detect within-subjects effects at 95% power. This seemingly low threshold reflects the statistical structure of multilevel models: within-subjects fixed effects are powered by Level-1 observations — here, 148 binary classification trials per participant — rather than by the number of Level-2 clusters. With 148 observations per person, detecting fixed effects on within-person variation achieves high power at small N; the final sample of *N* = 61 provides substantial additional power and enables detection of between-person individual differences. Power was prioritized for multilevel fixed effects; correlational analyses may be underpowered. For completeness, a sensitivity analysis indicates *N* = 61 can detect correlations of *r* ≥ .34 at 80% power (α = .05, two-tailed).

**Network Procedure**
We utilized a semantic dependency network of 147 traits constructed using data from 178 Amazon Mechanical Turk participants (25% consensus threshold). This network captures psychological implication structure (e.g., "If I am brave, I am adventurous") rather than linguistic co-occurrence. Static word embeddings (e.g., GloVe) are ill-suited for this purpose on two grounds: antonyms acquire high cosine similarity because they appear in identical sentence contexts, and cosine similarity is symmetric, discarding the directional dependencies (e.g., *Thoughtful* → *Humble* but not vice versa) that the dependency network preserves. From this network, we derived network-based Dice similarity (@eq-dice), representing the proportion of shared neighbors between traits.

$$S_{ij} = \frac{2|N(i) \cap N(j)|}{|N(i)| + |N(j)|}$$ {#eq-dice}

where $N(i)$ and $N(j)$ denote the neighbor sets of traits $i$ and $j$ in the semantic dependency network.

A visualization of the full semantic trait network is provided in Supplementary Materials F.

**Design**
*Training phase.* Participants self-evaluated approximately 60% of the network (90 traits) on a Likert scale from 1 (*Not at all*) to 7 (*Extremely*). Following a dot-estimation minimal group assignment task (NEST), participants were randomly assigned to be "overestimators" or "underestimators." In the *generalization phase*, participants classified all 148 traits in the network as characteristic of either the ingroup or outgroup (148 trials). This included 90 repeated traits and 58 novel traits.

During generalization phase, 90 traits are thus repeated while 58 traits are novel and never received a self-evaluation. Participants then proceed through all traits in the semantic trait network, and classify whether each trait is characteristic of the ingroup or the outgroup."

**Indices**
We computed *Similarity-to-Self* ($SS_g$; @eq-ss) as a similarity-weighted average of self-evaluations across training traits, capturing the degree to which the self-concept predicts the semantic neighborhood of each test trait. Results for a local self-concept clarity index (*H_g*) are reported in Supplementary Materials D.

$$SS_g = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T} E_t \cdot S_{tg}}{\sum_{t=1}^{T} S_{tg}}$$ {#eq-ss}

where $E_t$ is the self-evaluation on training trait $t$, $S_{tg}$ is the Dice similarity between training trait $t$ and test trait $g$, and $T$ is the number of training traits.

Each computational model produces a *model-derived Metacontrast Ratio* (MCR) as a generated quantity (see *Computational Modeling* below), computed using parameter-calibrated similarity weights and individual projection gradients: $\text{MCR}_t = \text{simW}_{\text{in},t} / \text{simW}_{\text{out},t}$, where $\text{simW}_{\text{in}}$ and $\text{simW}_{\text{out}}$ are the generalization-weighted sums of projection onto ingroup- and outgroup-predictive self-knowledge, respectively. The subject-level MCR ($\overline{\text{MCR}}_s$) averages this ratio across trials, yielding a person-specific index of how strongly the semantic self-concept discriminates ingroup from outgroup classification.

**Computational Modeling**
We compared four cognitive architectures based on category learning principles (Nosofsky, 2011) to test the representational structure of self-anchoring.

**Level 1: Bias Model (Motivational Baseline).** This model represents a general tendency to choose the ingroup regardless of trait content, serving as a baseline for ingroup favoritism:
$$P(\text{Ingroup} | g) = \text{logit}^{-1}(\text{logit}(\gamma))$$
where $\gamma$ is the bias parameter.

**Level 2: Symmetric Model (Traditional Self-Anchoring).** This model utilizes a single projection rate ($\alpha$) assuming that the rate of ingroup assimilation is mathematically identical to the rate of outgroup repulsion:
$$P(\text{Ingroup} | g) = \frac{\gamma \cdot (\sum_{t=1}^T S_{tg} \cdot G_t)^\beta}{\gamma \cdot (\sum_{t=1}^T S_{tg} \cdot G_t)^\beta + (1-\gamma) \cdot (\sum_{t=1}^T S_{tg} \cdot (1-G_t))^\beta}$$
where $G_t = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\alpha(E_t-4)}}$ represents the latent belief transformed from self-evaluations ($E_t$).

**Level 3: Symmetric + $\lambda$ Model (The Generalization Gradient).** This model introduces Shepard’s Law by adding a generalization sensitivity parameter ($\lambda$), representing the decay of inference across semantic similarity ($S_{tg} \rightarrow S_{tg}^\lambda$). This architecture treats $\lambda$ as a core parameter defining the structural reach of the self-concept, independent of social target or bias. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-05-lambda-identifiability
#| fig-cap: "How Shepard's Law (λ) Unlocks Parameter Identifiability. As λ increases, the generalization gradient becomes steeper, restricting the influence of self-evaluations to only local semantic neighbors. This 'flattening' of influence for more distant novel traits provides the mathematical leverage necessary to distinguish the structural reach of the self-concept (λ) from the extremity of social projection (α)."
#| eval: !expr file.exists(fig_path("fig05_lambda_identifiability.tiff"))
knitr::include_graphics(fig_path("fig05_lambda_identifiability.tiff"))
```

**Level 4: Asymmetric + $\lambda$ Model (The Full Architecture).** This model decouples the assimilation and repulsion processes into distinct parameters, $\alpha_{in}$ and $\alpha_{out}$, to test if social identity is driven by "ingroup love" or "outgroup hate":
$$G_{in,t} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\alpha_{in}(E_t-4)}} ; \quad G_{out,t} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{\alpha_{out}(E_t-4)}}$$
By utilizing novel traits to establish the baseline "semantic radius" via $\lambda$, the model possesses the mathematical leverage to decouple these otherwise collinear slopes, unlocking the asymmetric forces central to social identity theory. 

To ensure identifiability of these parameters within a 2AFC task, we leveraged three computational strategies. First, we exploited the unique information provided by novel versus repeated traits; while repeated traits primarily inform projection extremity ($\alpha$), novel traits isolate the signal for generalization sensitivity ($\lambda$) by forcing the model to rely entirely on the semantic similarity matrix ($S$). Second, we implemented the dual latent belief structure described above, allowing the model to distinguish choices driven by ingroup similarity from those driven by outgroup dissimilarity. Finally, we utilized hierarchical Bayesian regularization to stabilize individual estimates: by sharing statistical strength across participants, individual parameter estimates are shrunk toward the group mean, preventing extreme estimates from subjects with noisy or sparse data from distorting inference. To account for potential non-systematic noise in participant responses (e.g., accidental button presses or lapses in attention), we incorporated a lapse parameter ($w$) into all four architectures. This parameter estimates the probability that a given choice was a result of random guessing (fixed at $P = 0.5$) rather than the underlying cognitive model, such that the final probability of an ingroup choice is defined as:
$$P(\text{Ingroup}) = w \cdot 0.5 + (1 - w) \cdot P_{\text{model}}$$
This addition ensures that occasional outlying responses do not unduly bias the estimation of the structural parameters ($\lambda$, $\alpha$). Critically, $\gamma$ and $w$ are jointly identifiable because they exert influence at structurally distinct points on the choice function: $\gamma$ operates *inside* the logistic as an intercept shift, governing the response boundary when semantic evidence is ambiguous and balanced; $w$ operates *outside* the logistic, compressing only the asymptotes of the choice distribution and drawing its information from trials where the deterministic component predicts near-certainty but the participant responds inconsistently. Because each parameter leverages a different region of the psychometric function — the center versus the tails — they do not trade off in estimation. In addition to log-likelihood (used for LOO-CV model comparison), each model outputs, as generated quantities, trial-level predicted choice probabilities ($\hat{P}_t = w \cdot 0.5 + (1-w) \cdot P_{\text{model},t}$) and a model-derived Metacontrast Ratio ($\widehat{\text{MCR}}_t = \text{simW}_{in,t} / \text{simW}_{out,t}$), where $\text{simW}_{in,t}$ and $\text{simW}_{out,t}$ are the parameter-calibrated ingroup and outgroup similarity totals at trial $t$. This model-derived quantity is calibrated by each participant's posterior parameter estimates, incorporating both generalization breadth ($\lambda$) and projection slopes ($\alpha_{in}$, $\alpha_{out}$), making it person-specific: two participants with identical behavioral responses but different estimated parameters will yield different model MCRs, as the metric reflects each person's underlying representation of how strongly a given trait's semantic neighborhood predicts ingroup versus outgroup membership. This hierarchical structure was extended to a pooled analysis across all three studies, treating each study as an exchangeable sample of a broader human social-cognitive architecture (Global $\rightarrow$ Study $\rightarrow$ Subject). To ensure robust estimation across these distinct contexts, hierarchical variances were sampled from Cauchy distributions, providing the necessary regularization to accommodate the small hierarchical sample size. This architecture allowed for the formal estimation of "Global Mean" parameters ($\lambda$, $\alpha$, $w$) that capture cross-context structural properties of social generalization across the three intergroup contexts studied here. Models were fitted using Stan (four MCMC chains; 2,000 post-warmup samples per chain for individual-study models; 1,000 for the pooled three-level model). Convergence was confirmed via $\hat{R} < 1.01$ (Vehtari et al., 2021).

**Table 1. Summary of Computational Model Architectures.**

| Model | *k* | Parameters | Description |
|:------|:---:|:-----------|:------------|
| Bias | 2 | $\gamma$, $w$ | Ingroup favoritism baseline. Choices driven entirely by response bias; no role for trait similarity or self-knowledge. |
| Symmetric | 3 | $\alpha$, $\gamma$, $w$ | Single projection rate; ingroup assimilation and outgroup repulsion are mathematically yoked ($\alpha_{in} = \alpha_{out}$). |
| Symmetric+$\lambda$ | 4 | $\alpha$, $\gamma$, $\lambda$, $w$ | Adds Shepard's generalization gradient; the reach of the self-concept across semantic space is governed by a sensitivity parameter $\lambda$, but projection remains symmetric. |
| Asymmetric+$\lambda$ | 5 | $\alpha_{in}$, $\alpha_{out}$, $\gamma$, $\lambda$, $w$ | Full architecture. Decouples ingroup assimilation ($\alpha_{in}$) from outgroup repulsion ($\alpha_{out}$), allowing independent estimation of "ingroup love" and "outgroup hate." |

*Note.* $k$ = number of free parameters. $\alpha$ / $\alpha_{in}$ / $\alpha_{out}$ = projection rate(s) (0–10); $\gamma$ = response bias (0–1); $\lambda$ = generalization sensitivity (0–5); $w$ = lapse rate (0–1). All models estimated via hierarchical Bayesian inference; subject-level parameters are drawn from a group-level distribution with non-centered parameterization.

### Results
Predictors of ingroup classification were estimated using mixed-effects logistic regression with crossed random effects for subjects and traits; random slopes were estimated for focal predictors; in models testing cross-level interactions (a within-person predictor × between-person moderator), a random slope was always included for the level-1 predictor. Subject random intercepts account for baseline differences in individuals' overall tendency to select the ingroup regardless of trait content — capturing stable between-person variation in ingroup favoritism. Trait random intercepts account for baseline differences in how often a given trait is attributed to the ingroup regardless of who is rating it — capturing stable between-trait variation in perceived ingroup typicality. This structure ensures that fixed-effect estimates reflect within-person, within-trait associations rather than confounds from person-level response tendencies or trait-level ingroup stereotypicality. We report average marginal effects (AMEs) with 95% confidence intervals and two-tailed *p*-values. Desirability reliability was good, ICC(C, 16) = .682 [.601, .753].

**Predictors of Ingroup Classification**
Average marginal effects (AMEs) from mixed-effects logistic regression (desirability controlled in models for self-evaluations and similarity-to-self) quantified predictors of ingroup classification. Consistent with pre-registered predictions, a 1-SD increase in *Similarity-to-Self* increased P(ingroup) by 7.0 percentage points (AME = .070, 95% CI [.028, .111], *p* = .001), substantially larger than the 6.3 pp effect of direct self-evaluations (AME = .063, 95% CI [.040, .086], *p* < .001), replicating traditional self-anchoring. Desirability was non-significant (AME = .016, 95% CI [−.002, .034], *p* = .075). Across the Similarity-to-Self gradient, predicted P(ingroup) ranged from 48% at −1 SD to 56% at the mean to 64% at +1 SD. Also consistent with pre-registered predictions, the effect did not differ between trained and novel traits (Trained AME = .069, Novel AME = .073; difference = .004 pp, 95% CI [−.013, .020]), confirming practical equivalence and ruling out repetition as an explanation.

*SCT depersonalization and self-anchoring.* SCT predicts that stronger identifiers should show tighter alignment between self-ratings and ingroup classification, as depersonalization aligns self-beliefs with group-predictive attributes. We tested this with interaction terms (self-evaluation × SI; self-evaluation × Prototypicality; self-evaluation × SING.Ind) added to the primary classification model, with a random slope for self-evaluations by subject. None reached significance in Study 1: social identification (β = −.018, *z* = −0.30, *p* = .768), prototypicality (β = .014, *z* = 0.23, *p* = .820), independent self-construal (β = .036, *z* = 0.56, *p* = .573). In minimal groups, identification strength does not amplify the self-to-group classification link — consistent with the absence of group content that could anchor identification-based depersonalization.

*Trait segregation* (network nominal homophily) quantifies how much a participant's ingroup versus outgroup classifications cluster along the semantic similarity network—whether semantically connected traits tend to receive the same group label (*M* = .09, *SD* = .08; range [−.04, .26]). Higher values indicate that participants carved sharper, spatially coherent ingroup and outgroup regions out of the trait network; lower values indicate that ingroup and outgroup labels were intermixed across the semantic structure.

**Model Performance and Parameters**
We compared four cognitive architectures of social inference: Bias, Symmetric, Symmetric+$\lambda$, and Asymmetric+$\lambda$ (see Table 1 for architecture summary). Model selection used leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV; Vehtari et al., 2017), with models ranked by expected log predictive density (ELPD); $\Delta$ELPD is reported relative to the best-fitting model. Log-likelihood was stored at the trial level rather than the subject level, enabling observation-level LOO and reliable Pareto $k$ diagnostics; greater than 95% of trials had $k < 0.7$ across models, confirming the validity of the PSIS approximation (Vehtari et al., 2017). To complement the group-level comparison, we computed each participant's *per-subject LOO ELPD difference* (per-subject $\Delta$ELPD = $\text{ELPD}_{\text{asymmetric}} - \text{ELPD}_{\text{symmetric}}$), summing pointwise ELPD values across that participant's valid trials. A positive per-subject $\Delta$ELPD indicates the asymmetric architecture better predicts that individual's choices; a negative value indicates the symmetric architecture is favored. This person-specific index was examined against individual-difference measures to test whether particular psychological characteristics predict which model best accounts for a given participant's behavior.

**Table 2. LOO Model Comparison — Study 1 (Minimal Groups, *N* = 61).**

| Model | ELPD | SE | $\Delta$ELPD | $\Delta$SE |
|:------|-----:|---:|-------------:|----------:|
| Symmetric+$\lambda$ | −5647.5 | 29.2 | 0.0 | — |
| Asymmetric+$\lambda$* | −5647.7 | 29.1 | −0.21 | 0.55 |
| Symmetric | −5760.4 | 25.6 | −112.9 | 13.0 |
| Bias | −5839.0 | 24.7 | −191.4 | 16.2 |

*Note.* ELPD = expected log predictive density. $\Delta$ELPD relative to best-fitting model (row 1). Models ordered from best to worst fit. $|\Delta\text{ELPD}| > 2 \times \Delta\text{SE}$ is taken as meaningful difference in predictive accuracy. *One divergent transition; $\hat{R}_{\max} = 1.006$.

The Symmetric+$\lambda$ model provided the best predictive fit (ELPD = $-5647.5$, SE = $29.2$), meaningfully outperforming the Symmetric model ($\Delta$ELPD = $-112.9$, SE = $13.0$; $|\Delta\text{ELPD}|/\Delta\text{SE} = 8.7$) and the Bias model ($\Delta$ELPD = $-191.4$, SE = $16.2$). The Asymmetric+$\lambda$ model was statistically indistinguishable from the winner ($\Delta$ELPD = $-0.21$, SE = $0.55$; $|\Delta\text{ELPD}|/\Delta\text{SE} = 0.38$), while producing one divergent transition ($\hat{R}_{\max} = 1.006$). Together these results indicate that in minimal groups, decoupling ingroup projection ($\alpha_{in}$) from outgroup discrimination ($\alpha_{out}$) affords no reliable improvement in predictive accuracy: a symmetric projection rate captures the data as well as an asymmetric one. Group-level parameter medians for the Symmetric+$\lambda$ model were: projection rate $\alpha = 2.80$ (95% CI $[1.50, 6.67]$), generalization sensitivity $\lambda = 3.56$ (95% CI $[2.79, 4.22]$), ingroup classification baseline $\gamma = 0.36$ (95% CI $[0.28, 0.45]$), and lapse rate $w = 0.56$ (95% CI $[0.39, 0.70]$). The elevated lapse rate under minimal group conditions is interpretable rather than artifactual: when groups carry no prior content, a substantial portion of trial-by-trial variability is structurally underdetermined — participants must classify 148 traits for a group defined by nothing beyond an arbitrary assignment label, producing genuine choice indeterminacy the similarity structure cannot fully resolve. Importantly, $\alpha$ and $\lambda$ are estimated conditional on the non-lapse component of responses and are therefore not biased by high $w$; the lapse parameter absorbs residual variability rather than redistributing it onto structural estimates. Whether $w$ is lower in Studies 2 and 3 — where real group content provides richer classification cues — is itself a substantive question about how much of the self-concept's predictive signal depends on groups having meaningful identity content. For completeness, the Asymmetric+$\lambda$ model estimated $\alpha_{in} = 4.56$ (95% CI $[1.33, 9.41]$) and $\alpha_{out} = 3.16$ (95% CI $[1.96, 7.92]$); the wide, overlapping credible intervals reflect the model's inability to dissociate the two parameters reliably under minimal-group conditions.

The following individual-difference analyses are exploratory. We examined Pearson correlations between each model parameter ($m$, $\gamma$, $\lambda$, $w$) and the model-derived MCR against nine individual-difference scales (FDR correction applied separately for mechanism-personality tests [$k = 36$: $m$, $\gamma$, $\lambda$, MCR × 9 scales] and for ΔELPD-personality tests [$k = 9$]; $w$ reported descriptively). Structural parameters showed minimal associations: $m$, $\lambda$, and $w$ showed no nominal associations, and $\gamma$ showed no FDR-significant associations (best: SING.Inter $r = .27$, $p_{\text{raw}} = .039$, $p_{\text{FDR}} = .279$). The model-derived MCR—which integrates each participant's parameter estimates with their actual semantic self-structure into a person-specific discrimination index—was the strongest and most consistent predictor across scales. It survived FDR correction for SING independence ($r = .53$, $p_{\text{raw}} < .001$, $p_{\text{FDR}} < .001$), and showed nominal associations with SING interdependence ($r = .36$, $p_{\text{raw}} = .005$, $p_{\text{FDR}} = .085$), social identification ($r = .31$, $p_{\text{raw}} = .015$, $p_{\text{FDR}} = .170$), and perceived prototypicality ($r = .30$, $p_{\text{raw}} = .019$, $p_{\text{FDR}} = .170$). The divergence between the structural parameters and the MCR is theoretically informative: projection rate and generalization breadth appear to reflect relatively stable cognitive tendencies that do not vary strongly with social identity strength, while the MCR—by weighting those tendencies against each participant's actual semantic self-concept—captures the identity-relevant signal that scales with group attachment. The model-derived MCR thus captures identity-relevant individual variation in self-anchoring that the structural parameters alone do not.

We also computed the per-subject $\Delta$ELPD as an individual-level index of which model architecture better predicted each participant's choices ($\Delta$ELPD = ELPD$_{\text{asymmetric}}$ − ELPD$_{\text{symmetric}}$; positive values indicate the asymmetric model is better supported for that individual, negative values indicate the symmetric model is favored). Thirty of 61 participants showed positive $\Delta$ELPD (i.e., the asymmetric model better predicted their choices), consistent with the near-zero group-level difference (total $\Delta$ELPD = −0.21). $\Delta$ELPD was not reliably associated with any individual-difference scale (all *r*s ≤ .20, all *p*s ≥ .127 with FDR correction applied separately over the 9 ΔELPD-personality tests). In the minimal-group context, which model better fits an individual's choices does not meaningfully vary with their personality profile.

A pooled CCA combining all three studies (*N* = 507) is reported in Supplementary Materials E; individual-study CCAs are not reported given the sample-size constraints of single-study CCA with 15 variables.

### Discussion
Similarity-to-self predicted ingroup classification more strongly than one-to-one trait matching, confirming that self-anchoring is a structured inferential process rather than simple attribute replication. The effect held across both novel and repeated traits, ruling out repetition as an explanation. Model comparison revealed that the Symmetric+$\lambda$ architecture fit the data equivalently to the fully asymmetric model ($\Delta$ELPD = −0.21, SE = 0.55), indicating that in minimal groups, ingroup assimilation and outgroup discrimination are not architecturally dissociable — both are captured by a single projection rate. The model-derived MCR correlated with individual differences in group attachment, confirming that the computational index captures identity-relevant variation that structural parameters alone do not.

## STUDY 2: SELF-ANCHORING BASED ON RELATIVE STATUS OF UNIVERSITY GROUPS
Study 2 examined how social status modulates self-anchoring in real-world social categories. Study 2 was pre-registered at OSF (https://osf.io/q2vx7). We pre-registered the primary SS effect and its generalization to novel traits; a directional prediction that lower-status outgroup comparisons would produce stronger ingroup projection relative to negation (this prediction was disconfirmed — the high-status condition produced the strongest projection); that trait segregation would correlate positively with need to belong and dialectical self-views and negatively with self-esteem and independent self-construal; that self-anchoring strength would associate with social identification, perceived prototypicality, and status perceptions as tests of SCT's depersonalization account; and that generalization to novel traits would not differ from generalization to trained traits. Computational modeling analyses and MCR-based individual differences are exploratory. Minimal groups in Study 1 could not dissociate ingroup projection from outgroup discrimination—a symmetric architecture sufficed. Real social categories introduce meaningful intergroup history, perceived status differentials, and motivated distinctiveness concerns that should activate the two processes differentially. Under conditions of positive regard for the outgroup (e.g., a higher-status rival university), the prior motivation to classify traits as ingroup-characteristic (γ) may attenuate even while the projection mechanism (α) remains intact — or vice versa for derogated outgroups. Study 2 therefore tests both whether the asymmetric architecture is detectable under real intergroup conditions and whether status-modulated motivation manifests as changes in the projection rate or in the baseline ingroup preference.

Beyond the projection rate ($\alpha$), SCT's comparative fit principle predicts that categorization becomes most salient when intergroup differences are maximized relative to intragroup similarity (Turner et al., 1987). If $\lambda$ indexes the breadth of the self-concept's semantic reach, it may be sensitive to this contrast. As a non-preregistered exploratory test, we examined whether $\lambda$ varied across outgroup contrast conditions. The two directional predictions are: higher $\lambda$ (narrowing) in the high-status condition if participants restrict projection to guard against overlap with a prestigious outgroup; lower $\lambda$ (broadening) if intergroup salience expands the inferential gradient. Given the exploratory status and the expectation of small effects, these analyses should be interpreted with appropriate caution.

### Methods
From an initial pool of XX participants, XX were excluded (final *N* = 181).[^s2n]

[^s2n]: The Study 2 sample was initially reported as *N* = 283 based on the count of participants who completed initial consent and demographics. Subsequent inspection revealed that only 181 participants completed all task phases (training and generalization). The *N* = 181 is the sample for all analyses reported here and meets the 80% power threshold for detecting cross-level interactions at a small effect size. Exclusions were applied for: self-reported low task seriousness (*n* = 2), self-reported unusable data (*n* = 4), and careless responding — defined as > 80% identical self-evaluations, > 95% identical group classifications, or > 40% missing responses in either phase (*n* = 47). Participants were native English-speaking university students (XX% Cisgender Female, XX% Cisgender Male, XX% Nonbinary; *M*<sub>Age</sub> = XX, *SD*<sub>Age</sub> = XX, Range<sub>Age</sub> = [XX, XX]). Ethnic composition included XX% White, XX% Mixed, XX% Asian, XX% Hispanic, XX% Native-American, and XX% Black. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three outgroup contrast conditions: Negation ("Not Ingroup University"), Higher Status University, or Lower Status University. A *simr* power analysis indicated that our final sample (*N* = 181) meets the 80% power threshold for detecting a cross-level interaction between similarity-to-self and condition at a small effect size (log-odds β = .35; Green & MacLeod, 2016). Power was prioritized for multilevel fixed effects; correlational analyses may be underpowered. For completeness, a sensitivity analysis indicates *N* = 181 can detect correlations of *r* ≥ .20 at 80% power (α = .05, two-tailed).

### Results
**Manipulation Checks**
Manipulation checks confirmed perceived status differences. All participants rated the status and warmth of all three universities; pairwise contrasts used linear mixed models with subject random intercepts. Compared to the ingroup university (*M* = 6.24, *SD* = 1.36), the high-status university was rated significantly higher (*M* = 8.63, *SD* = 1.46, *p* < .001) and the low-status university significantly lower (*M* = 4.71, *SD* = 1.40, *p* < .001). Participants felt most warmly toward the ingroup (*M* = .783, *SD* = .156), followed by the high-status (*M* = .680, *SD* = .226, *p* < .001) and low-status university (*M* = .466, *SD* = .227, *p* < .001; warmth on 0–1 scale).

**Predictors of Ingroup Classification**
Average marginal effects (AMEs) from mixed-effects logistic regression (desirability controlled in focal predictor models) quantified ingroup classification. Consistent with pre-registered predictions, a 1-SD increase in Similarity-to-Self increased P(ingroup choice) by 6.3 pp (AME = .063, 95% CI [.036, .090], *p* < .001); direct self-evaluations showed a 4.8 pp effect (AME = .048, 95% CI [.036, .061], *p* < .001), and desirability showed a 4.7 pp effect (AME = .048, 95% CI [.034, .061], *p* < .001). Effects for Similarity-to-Self varied by outgroup: the effect was significant in the negation condition (AME = .046, 95% CI [.013, .081], *p* = .007) and strongly so in the high-status condition (AME = .100, 95% CI [.047, .153], *p* < .001), but non-significant in the low-status condition (AME = .044, 95% CI [−.006, .094], *p* = .082). Across the Similarity-to-Self gradient in the negation condition, predicted P(ingroup) ranged from 61% at −1 SD to 68% at the mean to 73% at +1 SD; in the high-status condition, the range was considerably wider: 40% to 51% to 60%. A three-way model (Similarity-to-Self × Novel × Outgroup) examined whether generalization varied by outgroup condition. In the negation condition, effects were significant for both trained (AME = .049, 95% CI [.014, .083], *p* = .006) and novel traits (AME = .043, 95% CI [.008, .077], *p* = .015), suggesting self-anchoring generalizes to novel traits when contrasting against a neutral outgroup. The high-status condition showed the strongest generalization, with large significant effects for trained (AME = .104, 95% CI [.049, .158], *p* < .001) and novel traits (AME = .097, 95% CI [.043, .151], *p* < .001). The low-status condition again showed attenuation, with non-significant trained effects (AME = .047, 95% CI [−.003, .098], *p* = .064) and non-significant novel-trait effects (AME = .040, 95% CI [−.012, .091], *p* = .133), suggesting generalization may be selectively suppressed when the outgroup is perceived as lower status.
*SCT depersonalization and self-anchoring.* As a pre-registered test of SCT's depersonalization prediction (H6), we examined whether stronger identifiers show tighter alignment between self-ratings and ingroup classification. The same interaction tests (self-evaluation × SI; self-evaluation × Prototypicality; self-evaluation × SING.Ind; random slope for self-evaluations by subject) were significant for social identification (β = .090, *z* = 2.66, *p* = .008) and perceived prototypicality (β = .079, *z* = 2.33, *p* = .020). Independent self-construal was not significant (β = .053, *z* = 1.54, *p* = .123). When groups carry real identity content, stronger identifiers and those who perceive themselves as more prototypical ingroup members show a reliably stronger self-to-classification link — consistent with SCT's depersonalization account.

**Trait Segregation**
Trait segregation analyses showed that high-status contrast participants segregated traits more (*M* = .11, *SD* = .08) than low-status (*M* = .05) or negation (*M* = .04) participants—perceiving a more prestigious outgroup appears to sharpen the categorical boundaries participants drew between ingroup and outgroup trait profiles.

**Generalization Model**

**Table 3. LOO Model Comparison — Study 2 (University Status Groups, *N* = 181).**

| Model | ELPD | SE | $\Delta$ELPD | $\Delta$SE |
|:------|-----:|---:|-------------:|----------:|
| Sym+$\lambda$ | −15,906.09 | 63.36 | 0.0 | — |
| Asym+$\lambda$ | −15,907.36 | 63.28 | −1.27 | 2.48 |
| Symmetric | −16,133.31 | 60.20 | −227.21 | 20.29 |
| Bias | −16,299.15 | 59.29 | −393.05 | 25.56 |

*Note.* ELPD = expected log predictive density. $\Delta$ELPD relative to best-fitting model (row 1). Sym+$\lambda$ and Asym+$\lambda$ are statistically indistinguishable ($\Delta$ELPD = −1.27, SE = 2.48); the simpler Sym+$\lambda$ is preferred by parsimony.

The self-projection models (Sym+$\lambda$, Asym+$\lambda$) substantially outperformed the Symmetric and Bias architectures across all conditions (see Table 3). As in Study 1, Sym+$\lambda$ and Asym+$\lambda$ were statistically indistinguishable overall ($\Delta$ELPD = −1.27, SE = 2.48), favoring the simpler symmetric architecture by parsimony. Per-condition model comparisons reveal a theoretically interpretable pattern: in the Negation condition (abstract outgroup "Not UCR"), Asym+$\lambda$ was numerically preferred ($\Delta$ELPD = +2.95 in favor of Asym+$\lambda$ over Sym+$\lambda$); in the High-Status condition, Sym+$\lambda$ was preferred ($\Delta$ELPD = +3.96); and in the Low-Status condition, architectures were essentially tied ($\Delta$ELPD = +0.26). The asymmetric advantage was significantly greater in the Negation condition than the High-Status condition ($\Delta\Delta$ELPD = 0.114, *t*(109) = 2.16, *p* = .033), suggesting that when the outgroup is concrete and positively-regarded, symmetric processing of in- and outgroup information is more strongly supported.

The primary parameter difference across conditions was not in the projection rate ($\alpha$; *F*(2, 178) = 0.33, *p* = .720) but in ingroup classification bias ($\gamma$). Participants in the High-Status condition showed dramatically reduced ingroup bias ($M$ = 0.36, *SD* = 0.19) relative to both Negation ($M$ = 0.60, *SD* = 0.23; $\beta$ = −0.246, *t*(178) = −6.65, *p* < .001) and Low-Status ($M$ = 0.61, *SD* = 0.20; *p* = .876 for Low-Status vs. Negation) participants. The Metacontrast Ratio was also lower in the High-Status condition ($M$ = 3.85, *SD* = 2.61) than in Negation ($M$ = 6.46, *SD* = 9.34; $\beta$ = −2.61, *t*(178) = −2.26, *p* = .025). Individual-level MCR correlated with RSE (*r* = .363, *p*<sub>FDR</sub> < .001), Prototypicality (*r* = .260, *p*<sub>FDR</sub> = .004), SING.Ind (*r* = .292, *p*<sub>FDR</sub> = .001), NFC (*r* = .292, *p*<sub>FDR</sub> = .001), and Social Identification (*r* = .224, *p*<sub>FDR</sub> = .015); generalization breadth ($\lambda$) independently correlated with Social Identification (*r* = .246, *p*<sub>FDR</sub> = .007). The ingroup bias parameter $\gamma$ showed no FDR-significant personality associations (all *p*<sub>FDR</sub> > .50).

*Comparative fit and generalization sensitivity.* As a non-preregistered exploratory analysis, we tested whether $\lambda$ differed across outgroup contrast conditions using a linear model ($\lambda \sim \text{condition}$). As noted above, both a higher $\lambda$ (narrowing as boundary protection) and a lower $\lambda$ (broadening as depersonalization) in the high-status condition are interpretable under SCT. $\lambda$ differed significantly across conditions (*F*(2, 178) = 3.64, *p* = .028, *R*² = .039), though differences were numerically small on the 0–5 scale. The Low-Status condition showed slightly narrower generalization than Negation ($M_{\text{Low}}$ = 3.47, *SD* = 0.10 vs. $M_{\text{Neg}}$ = 3.53, *SD* = 0.15; $\beta$ = −0.063, *t*(178) = −2.68, *p* = .008); the High-Status condition was intermediate and did not differ significantly from Negation ($M_{\text{High}}$ = 3.50, *SD* = 0.13; *p* = .127). The direction in the Low-Status condition—slight generalization contraction—is consistent with a meta-contrast sharpening account: a derogated outgroup makes categorical boundaries more salient, narrowing the scope of self-concept generalization. At the individual level, $\lambda$ correlated positively with outgroup warmth in the High-Status condition (*r* = .272, 95% CI [.007, .501], *p* = .045, *n* = 55) but not in the Low-Status condition (*r* = .055, *p* = .715, *n* = 46); overall the correlation was non-significant (*r* = .121, *p* = .229). The positive warmth–$\lambda$ association in the High-Status condition suggests that individuals who regard the prestigious outgroup more favorably generalize their self-concept more broadly during ingroup classification, consistent with reduced categorical rigidity when intergroup boundaries are perceived as permeable.

*Positive distinctiveness and ingroup bias.* If γ operationalizes the positive distinctiveness motive at the individual level, participants who view the higher-status outgroup more warmly should show attenuated ingroup bias. We tested this with Spearman's ρ between individual-level γ and outgroup warmth within each condition. The association was positive and directionally non-significant in the High-Status condition (ρ = .233, *n* = 55, *p* = .088) and null in the Low-Status condition (ρ = .208, *n* = 46, *p* = .166). The condition-level γ attenuation (High-Status *M* = 0.36 vs. Negation *M* = 0.60) is therefore a uniform structural shift — present for everyone in the High-Status condition — rather than a within-condition effect driven by individual variation in outgroup attitudes.

### Discussion
Study 2 replicates similarity-based generalization in real-world social categories while revealing critical contextual modulations based on perceived social status. The primary computational finding is not an attenuation of the projection rate itself—$\alpha$ did not differ across conditions—but a dramatic reduction in the ingroup classification bias parameter ($\gamma$) when contrasting against the higher-status outgroup. Participants facing UCLA as their outgroup were less disposed to classify traits as ingroup-characteristic, suggesting that when the outgroup is positively-regarded and prestigious, the pull toward ingroup-exclusive attribution weakens. The projection mechanism (how self-attributes map to ingroup estimates via semantic similarity) remains intact; what changes is the prior disposition to choose the ingroup. The per-condition model comparisons reinforce this: the asymmetric architecture provided no benefit in the High-Status condition (Sym+$\lambda$ preferred), consistent with symmetric in/outgroup processing when the outgroup is positively-regarded. The behavioral AMEs reveal a complementary pattern at the low-status end: similarity-to-self was attenuated when comparing against the perceived lower-status outgroup (AME = .044, *p* = .082), with generalization to novel traits also non-significant. Self-Categorization Theory's meta-contrast principle offers an interpretation: when an outgroup is perceived as occupying a lower position in the societal status hierarchy, the categorical boundary may already be rendered salient through status cues, reducing the need for self-similarity to serve as an additional discriminating signal. The slight narrowing of generalization breadth ($\lambda$) in the Low-Status condition ($M$ = 3.47 vs. Negation $M$ = 3.53, *p* = .008) corroborates this account at the computational level. Social Identity Theory's positive distinctiveness principle provides a related account: when positive ingroup distinctiveness is already established through perceived status differences, the motivational pressure to deploy self-referential inference may be reduced. Together, these results suggest that self-anchoring functions as a context-sensitive inference strategy — most active when the categorization problem is motivationally engaged but not structurally resolved by status alone. The robust MCR–social identification correlation (*r* = .224, *p*<sub>FDR</sub> = .015) confirms that the semantic contrast ratio captures the strength of an individual's psychological ingroup attachment.

It is worth emphasizing that the γ–α dissociation was not the anticipated locus of contextual modulation—a priori, the projection rate (α) was the theoretically expected lever by which status context would exert its effects on self-anchoring. The finding that α remained invariant while γ shifted dramatically is therefore a post-hoc observation, albeit a theoretically clarifying one: it suggests that the inferential machinery of self-anchoring (how self-beliefs convert into ingroup beliefs via semantic similarity) is a surprisingly stable cognitive process, while the motivational prior that orients that machinery (the baseline attraction toward ingroup classification) is the context-sensitive component. This distinction—between process stability and motivational variability—has been largely implicit in social identity theory, and the present formal architecture makes it empirically tractable for the first time.

Notably, the magnitude of γ in the High-Status condition (*M* ≈ 0.36) converges precisely with the group-level posterior from Study 1 (*M* ≈ 0.36), despite very different intergroup contexts. This numerical convergence suggests that a concrete, positively-regarded, high-status outgroup can functionally neutralize the baseline ingroup preference that even purely arbitrary minimal groups produce—effectively resetting the motivational prior to its floor, as if the intergroup distinction carries no additional ingroup-pull beyond the bare fact of categorical membership. Put differently, the mere existence of a group boundary is sufficient to generate modest ingroup preference (Study 1); a high-status outgroup is sufficient to erase it.

## STUDY 3: SELF-ANCHORING BASED ON RELATIVE SIZE OF RACIAL GROUPS
Study 3 applied the self-anchoring framework to racial identities (Asian and Latino participants), examining how majority or minority outgroup contrasts exert differential effects on generalization. Study 3 was not formally pre-registered. It was designed as a conceptual replication and boundary-condition test of Study 2, following the same theoretical predictions: that SS predicts ingroup classification and generalizes to novel traits, that intergroup context modulates the parameters of that process, and that MCR correlates with individual differences in group identification. Analyses labeled "exploratory" below go beyond this confirmatory scope.

### Methods
From an initial pool of 313 participants, 48 were excluded (final *N* = 265). Exclusions were applied for: self-reported low task seriousness (*n* = 2), self-reported unusable data (*n* = 9), and careless responding — defined as > 80% identical self-evaluations, > 95% identical group classifications, or > 40% missing responses in either phase (*n* = 37). Participants were native English-speaking university students (59.14% Cisgender Female, 40.86% Cisgender Male; *M*<sub>Age</sub> = 19.01, *SD*<sub>Age</sub> = 1.71, Range<sub>Age</sub> = [17, 33]), and were 50.97% Hispanic/Latino and 49.03% Asian. Participants were assigned to either a Minority (Asian vs. Latino) or Majority (Ingroup vs. White) comparison condition. Study 3 uses two conditions rather than Study 2's three, requiring a smaller sample for equivalent power; *N* = 265 comfortably exceeds the Study 2 power threshold for detecting a cross-level interaction at a small effect size (log-odds β = .35; Green & MacLeod, 2016). Power was prioritized for multilevel fixed effects; correlational analyses may be underpowered. For completeness, a sensitivity analysis indicates *N* = 265 can detect correlations of *r* ≥ .17 at 80% power (α = .05, two-tailed).

### Results
**Manipulation Checks**
All participants rated the status and warmth of White, Asian, and Latino groups; pairwise contrasts used linear mixed models with subject random intercepts. White groups were perceived as significantly higher status (*M* = 8.42, *SD* = 1.63) than Asian (*M* = 6.73, *SD* = 1.51, *p* < .001) or Latino (*M* = 5.02, *SD* = 1.59, *p* < .001) groups; Asian groups were also rated higher in status than Latino groups (*p* < .001). Warmth ratings (0–1 scale) were higher for Latino (*M* = .79, *SD* = .19) and Asian (*M* = .77, *SD* = .19) groups than for White groups (*M* = .54, *SD* = .23; all *p*s < .001); Latino and Asian warmth did not significantly differ (*p* = .245).

```{r}
#| eval: !expr file.exists(fig_path("fig10_manipulation_checks.tiff"))
knitr::include_graphics(fig_path("fig10_manipulation_checks.tiff"))
```

**Predictors of Ingroup Classification**
Average marginal effects (AMEs) from mixed-effects logistic regression (desirability controlled in focal predictor models) revealed that Similarity-to-Self did not predict ingroup classification overall (AME = .012, 95% CI [−.011, .036], *p* = .307). This null overall effect concealed condition-specific variation: the effect was absent in the minority-outgroup condition (AME = −.008, 95% CI [−.042, .026], *p* = .653) but significant in the majority-outgroup condition (AME = .034, 95% CI [.002, .066], *p* = .037). In the majority condition, predicted P(ingroup) ranged from 57% at −1 SD to 61% at the mean to 65% at +1 SD; in the minority condition the gradient was essentially flat (56.7%, 56.5%, 55.9%). Self-evaluations showed a robust overall effect (AME = .039, 95% CI [.028, .050], *p* < .001), as did desirability (AME = .032, 95% CI [.016, .047], *p* < .001). A three-way model (Similarity-to-Self × Novel × Condition) examined whether the majority-condition effect generalized to novel traits. In the majority condition, the trained-trait effect remained significant (AME = .040, 95% CI [.007, .072], *p* = .017), while the novel-trait effect was positive but non-significant (AME = .026, 95% CI [−.007, .058], *p* = .125). In the minority condition, neither trained nor novel-trait effects were significant (AME = −.009, *p* = .603; AME = −.006, *p* = .729). These patterns suggest that in the racial context, similarity-based inference is present for familiar traits when contrasting against the majority, but does not reliably propagate to semantically novel traits. Results from the computational model are reported in the Generalization Model section below, along with canonical correlation results.

*SCT depersonalization and self-anchoring.* The analogous interaction tests were null across all three moderators in Study 3: social identification (β = .027, *z* = 0.96, *p* = .336), prototypicality (β = .040, *z* = 1.46, *p* = .144), independent self-construal (β = .038, *z* = 1.39, *p* = .163). The elevated lapse rate (*w* = 0.64) in Study 3 likely reduces behavioral leverage for detecting identification-based modulation of the self-to-group mapping; the self-anchoring signal is noisier in racial contexts, attenuating the interaction's detectability.

**Trait Segregation**
Minority contrast participants segregated traits significantly more (*M* = .12, *SD* = .08) than majority contrast participants (*M* = .08, *p* < .001). This is superficially opposite to Study 2, where high-status contrast produced greater segregation than the other conditions — but the underlying pattern is identical across both studies: the condition associated with *less* self-projection is also the condition with *more* trait segregation. In Study 2, contrasting against a high-status outgroup suppressed self-projection and elevated segregation; in Study 3, contrasting against a fellow minority group suppressed self-projection and elevated segregation. In both cases, when the intergroup context reduces the self-concept's organizational leverage over classification, participants fall back on coarser, more rigid categorical partitioning rather than semantically structured inference.


**Generalization Model**

**Table 4. LOO Model Comparison — Study 3 (Racial Group Size, *N* = 265).**

| Model | ELPD | SE | $\Delta$ELPD | $\Delta$SE |
|:------|-----:|---:|-------------:|----------:|
| Sym+$\lambda$ | −24,573.70 | 58.56 | 0.0 | — |
| Asym+$\lambda$ | −24,575.83 | 58.53 | −2.13 | 1.20 |
| Symmetric | −24,813.25 | 53.77 | −239.55 | 21.45 |
| Bias | −25,019.26 | 52.67 | −445.57 | 27.06 |

*Note.* ELPD = expected log predictive density. $\Delta$ELPD relative to best-fitting model (row 1).

As in Studies 1 and 2, the Sym+$\lambda$ model provided the best fit ($\Delta$ELPD = 0; reference). The Asym+$\lambda$ model was statistically indistinguishable (ΔELPD = −2.13, SE = 1.20; ratio = 1.78), and models with a generalization sensitivity parameter substantially outperformed architectures without one (Symmetric: ΔELPD = −239.55, SE = 21.45; Bias: ΔELPD = −445.57, SE = 27.06). Per-subject ELPD by condition showed no differential advantage for Asym+$\lambda$ in either the Minority (mean ΔELPD = −0.010, *t*(137) = −1.13, *p* = .262) or Majority (mean ΔELPD = −0.006, *t*(126) = −0.73, *p* = .466) condition, and these did not differ from each other (ΔΔELPD = −0.003, *t*(262) = −0.26, *p* = .794). Symmetric projection was therefore sufficient across both racial contrast conditions.

Group-level back-transformed parameters from the winning Sym+$\lambda$ model were: projection rate $\alpha$ = 2.27 [1.67, 3.20], ingroup bias $\gamma$ = 0.59 [0.53, 0.67], generalization sensitivity $\lambda$ = 3.50 [3.12, 4.04], and lapse rate $w$ = 0.64 [0.56, 0.71]. Neither projection rate ($\alpha$: F(1, 263) = 0.19, *p* = .667; Minority *M* = 2.28, Majority *M* = 2.27) nor ingroup bias ($\gamma$: F(1, 263) = 1.84, *p* = .177; Minority *M* = 0.53, Majority *M* = 0.57) differed by condition. The lapse rate $w$ was modestly higher in the Minority condition (Minority *M* = 0.64 vs. Majority *M* = 0.56; F(1, 263) = 4.62, *p* = .033, R² = .017), indicating that minority–minority contrast participants showed somewhat less deterministic classification overall. The semantic contrast ratio (MCR) did not differ by condition (Minority *M* = 6.22 vs. Majority *M* = 6.49; F(1, 263) = 0.08, *p* = .780).

FDR-corrected correlations between model-derived MCR and individual differences revealed that MCR was positively associated with independent self-construal (SING.Ind: *r* = .349, *p*~FDR~ < .001), self-esteem (RSE: *r* = .309, *p*~FDR~ < .001), self-concept clarity (SCC: *r* = .214, *p*~FDR~ = .005), and social identification (SI: *r* = .172, *p*~FDR~ = .025), and negatively associated with dialectical self-views (DS: *r* = −.212, *p*~FDR~ = .005). The ingroup bias parameter $\gamma$ showed FDR-significant personality associations in Study 3, in contrast to its null pattern in Studies 1 and 2: higher self-esteem predicted lower ingroup bias (RSE: *r* = −.191, *p*~FDR~ = .014), higher self-concept clarity predicted lower ingroup bias (SCC: *r* = −.185, *p*~FDR~ = .016), more dialectical self-views predicted higher ingroup bias (DS: *r* = .182, *p*~FDR~ = .017), and stronger need to belong predicted higher ingroup bias (NTB: *r* = .163, *p*~FDR~ = .033). These associations suggest that in racial contexts, where group boundaries carry real-world valence, the positive distinctiveness motive is more strongly linked to self-concept organization: individuals with more stable, clearly bounded self-concepts show less categorical favoritism, while those with more ambivalent self-structures and stronger affiliation needs show more. No other theoretical parameters ($\alpha$, $\lambda$, ΔELPD) survived FDR correction; generalization sensitivity $\lambda$ was not associated with self-concept clarity ($r$ = .062, *p* = .319), indicating that broader semantic projection does not co-occur with clearer self-organization in racial contexts.
*Comparative fit and generalization sensitivity.* As a non-preregistered exploratory analysis, we tested whether $\lambda$ differed between the majority and minority contrast conditions ($\lambda \sim \text{condition}$). Unlike Study 2, where the Low-Status condition showed a small but significant reduction in $\lambda$, generalization sensitivity was identical across conditions in Study 3 (Minority *M* = 3.49, Majority *M* = 3.49; F(1, 263) = 0.26, *p* = .611). Generalization breadth was not modulated by racial outgroup contrast type. At the individual level, $\lambda$ was positively associated with ingroup-relative preference (own-minority preference over other-minority; *r* = .147, *p* = .024), driven primarily by the Majority condition (*r* = .215, *p* = .023; Minority: *r* = .094, *p* = .302; interaction *p* = .314). Participants who feel more strongly that their own racial group is preferable to the other minority group project their self-concept more broadly when their contrast is against White — consistent with stronger group identification amplifying the reach of self-anchoring.

*Intergroup preference and ingroup bias.* A significant condition × ingroup-over-majority preference interaction emerged for $\gamma$ (F(1, 225) = 4.32, *p* = .039): in the Majority condition, stronger preference for own minority over White (*r*= .171, *p* = .074) was directionally associated with higher ingroup classification bias, while in the Minority condition this association was absent or reversed (*r* = −.108, *p* = .244). The pattern indicates that when participants are contrasting their own group against the racial majority, those who feel more strongly that their group is better than Whites also classify more traits as ingroup — consistent with activated positive distinctiveness motivations driving both affective and cognitive ingroup favoritism simultaneously.

*Race of participant as a moderator.* The overall condition effects on $\gamma$ were significantly moderated by participant race (F(1, 261) = 6.53, *p* = .011). Asian participants showed higher ingroup classification bias in the Minority condition ($M$ = 0.69) than the Majority condition ($M$ = 0.63), while Latino participants showed the opposite pattern (Minority $M$ = 0.41, Majority $M$ = 0.50; Majority condition *p* = .032). Within the Minority condition, Asian participants exhibited substantially higher ingroup bias than Latino participants, despite both groups facing a structurally symmetrical contrast. This asymmetry is not unexpected: within the same Asian-vs-Latino contrast, Asians and Latinos occupy reversed ingroup/outgroup roles, and the two groups may differ in their baseline readiness to use racial self-categorization as a classification heuristic. The lapse rate condition effect (Minority > Majority) was driven entirely by Latino participants (within-Latino: *p* = .021; within-Asian: *p* = .360). Stratifying the MCR–personality correlations by race revealed that the MCR–prototypicality association observed in Study 2 replicated for Latino participants (*r* = .227, *p* = .009) but not Asian participants (*r* = −.028, *p* = .753; Fisher *z* = −2.06, *p* = .039). MCR–self-esteem (RSE) and MCR–independent self-construal (SING.Ind) were significant in both racial groups (*r*s ≥ .203, *p*s ≤ .022). A full breakdown of condition × race interactions for all parameters is provided in Supplementary Materials C.

*Self-as-prototype and projection.* To test SCT's self-as-prototype assumption, we examined whether perceived prototypicality (Proto) predicted individual projection rates ($\alpha$) and whether this association differed by contrast condition ($\alpha \sim \text{Proto} \times \text{condition}$). The interaction was null (F(1, 256) = 0.13, *p* = .721), and Proto showed no association with $\alpha$ in either condition (Minority: *r* = .030, *p* = .724; Majority: *r* = −.015, *p* = .871). Perceived prototypicality did not modulate projection rate in the racial context, consistent with the pattern across Studies 1 and 2 where prototypicality correlated with MCR but not $\alpha$ directly.

### Discussion
Study 3 extends self-anchoring to the racial context, revealing that similarity-based projection is activated when minority participants contrast their ingroup against the dominant White majority but is absent when contrasting against a fellow minority group. The behavioral AMEs showed no overall effect of similarity-to-self (AME = .012, *p* = .307), with the effect concentrated in the majority-outgroup condition (AME = .034, *p* = .037) and absent in the minority-outgroup condition (AME = −.008, *p* = .653). The computational model largely mirrored this pattern, with one notable addition: the lapse rate $w$ was modestly higher in the Minority condition (Minority *M* = 0.64 vs. Majority *M* = 0.56; *p* = .033), indicating less deterministic classification when contrasting against a fellow minority group. Neither the projection rate $\alpha$ nor ingroup bias $\gamma$ differed by condition as main effects (*p*s > .177), though the $\gamma$ null was qualified by a significant condition × participant race interaction — and — unlike Study 2 — the generalization sensitivity $\lambda$ was identical across conditions (*p* = .611). The Sym+$\lambda$ architecture was again sufficient; no improvement from allowing asymmetric projection was observed in either condition. This provides further evidence that the suppression of self-anchoring in the minority-minority contrast is not due to a reduction in projection rate or a narrowing of generalization breadth, but to an increase in response stochasticity — suggesting that the contrast problem itself is less tractable under fellow-minority comparison. MCR correlated with independent self-construal, self-esteem, self-concept clarity, and social identification (all *p*~FDR~ ≤ .025), replicating the MCR-personality structure from Study 2 in a racial group context.

Self-Categorization Theory provides two complementary interpretations. First, the meta-contrast principle predicts that a categorization becomes psychologically active when perceived intergroup differences exceed intragroup differences. Contrasting a minority group against the dominant majority group instantiates a salient, high-stakes categorical boundary — one that status perceptions alone cannot resolve — motivating the use of self-anchoring to define and stabilize ingroup identity. When contrasting against a fellow minority group, by contrast, the two groups share a superordinate social position in the broader racial hierarchy, which may invoke a sense of common fate and blur the functional distinctiveness of the between-minority boundary. Under this interpretation, the self-concept does not serve as a reliable prototype for one minority against another, because the shared minority status diminishes the meta-contrast. Second, the positive distinctiveness principle suggests that the motivation to differentiate one's ingroup is strongest against a more powerful outgroup — where distinctiveness must be actively constructed — and weakest when the comparison itself makes ingroup superiority on the relevant dimension ambiguous.

*Race moderation.* The condition × race interaction on $\gamma$ reveals that the Minority condition is not psychologically equivalent for Asian and Latino participants: the two groups play structurally opposite roles (one is always the ingroup, the other the outgroup), and their ingroup bias reflects this. Asian participants showed higher ingroup classification bias when the outgroup was Latino ($M$ = 0.69) than when it was White ($M$ = 0.63); Latino participants showed the reverse, with higher bias against White ($M$ = 0.50) than against Asian ($M$ = 0.41). One reading of this pattern is racial identification asymmetry: Asians in this sample may have stronger within-minority boundary sensitivity (or weaker common-fate identification with Latinos), while Latinos show stronger ingroup-outgroup accentuation when the outgroup is the dominant racial majority. The MCR–prototypicality association also diverged by race: it replicated in Latino participants but was absent in Asians. If prototypicality indexes how representative one's individual traits are of the ingroup, this replication for Latinos — but not Asians — may reflect differences in the degree to which racial identity is organized around self-concept overlap versus other sources (e.g., shared adversity, language, cultural practice). These patterns are exploratory, and should be interpreted cautiously given cell sizes of 56–79 participants. The supplementary materials provide full parameter tables stratified by condition and race.

Regarding generalization, formal tests (Similarity-to-Self × Novel × Condition) showed that neither trained nor novel-trait effects were significant in the minority condition (both *p*s > .60). In the majority condition, the trained-trait effect was significant (AME = .040, *p* = .017), while the novel-trait effect was positive but non-significant (AME = .026, *p* = .125). Although formal generalization was not supported even in the majority condition, it is notable that both the trained and novel-trait AMEs were numerically larger in the majority condition than in the minority condition, consistent with a gradient of self-anchoring strength rather than a categorical absence of generalization.

*Warmth, generalization breadth, and ingroup bias.* Two intergroup preference variables modulated distinct computational parameters. Stronger own-minority preference over the other minority ($\lambda$ × inMinorityTherm: *r* = .215 in Majority condition) predicted broader self-concept generalization — consistent with participants who maintain clear within-minority group boundaries projecting their self-concept more widely when the contrast shifts to the racial majority. The relationship appears specific to the majority-outgroup condition: when participants contrast against Whites, having a sharper intragroup affective boundary (preferring own minority over the other) amplifies rather than constrains the generalization reach. This could reflect the role of group-identity coherence in self-anchoring: participants with well-defined minority identities (marked by both group loyalty and inter-minority distinction) may draw on a more organized and generative self-concept when the categorization task activates cross-racial boundaries. Separately, stronger preference for own minority over White ($\gamma$ × inMajorityTherm) predicted higher ingroup classification bias in the Majority condition (*p* = .039), a pattern absent in the Minority condition. Higher ingroup bias (γ) reflects a stronger prior for classifying traits as ingroup regardless of their similarity to self. When participants feel more strongly that their minority group surpasses the racial majority, this evaluative ingroup advantage appears to function as a classification prior — they default to ingroup assignment more strongly, independent of trait similarity. Together these two patterns suggest the warmth-to-behavior pathway in self-anchoring is decomposable: within-minority affective distinctions modulate the breadth of self-concept projection (λ), while cross-racial evaluative comparisons modulate the motivational prior for ingroup preference (γ). This mirrors the theoretical decomposition proposed by the model: inferential reach and ingroup preference are separable, and different aspects of intergroup affect differentially recruit these components.

*Study 2 versus Study 3: Why did generalization attenuate under racial group contrasts?* In Study 2, similarity-based generalization to novel traits was robust in the negation and high-status conditions. In Study 3, trained-trait effects were significant only in the majority condition and did not reliably extend to novel traits in either condition. One interpretation is that racial categories carry more pre-structured, culturally ingrained content than university affiliations: participants already hold clear expectations about which traits "belong" to racial ingroups and outgroups, leaving less room for flexible self-based inference to shape classification. van Veelen et al. (2017) proposed that self-anchoring is most active when people face genuine uncertainty about their group's content — when group membership is newly formed or contested. University groups provide relatively thin stereotypic content, making participants reliant on self-referential inference; racial groups come pre-loaded with cultural stereotypes that may preempt or compete with self-anchoring as a classification strategy. Consistent with this, the computational model found the lapse rate $w$ was higher in Study 3 overall ($M$ = 0.64) compared to Studies 1 ($M$ = 0.56) and 2 ($M$ = 0.56), suggesting that racial classification is more probabilistic and noisy — less driven by the clean semantic self-concept signal that powers generalization. When self-concept inference contributes a noisier signal against a backdrop of entrenched categorical knowledge, generalization to semantically similar but untrained traits is less likely to emerge reliably. The replication of MCR–personality correlations across all three studies confirms that self-anchoring remains operative as an individual-difference tendency; the group-level suppression of generalization in Study 3 may reflect contextual competition rather than a categorical absence of the mechanism.

## POOLED ANALYSIS: A UNIVERSAL LAW OF SOCIAL GENERALIZATION

To formally test whether the self-anchoring architecture generalizes across intergroup contexts, we fit the four hierarchical models to the combined sample across Studies 1–3 (*N* = 507) using a three-level hierarchy (Global $\rightarrow$ Study $\rightarrow$ Subject). This architecture estimates global population parameters ($\lambda$, $\alpha_{in}$, $\alpha_{out}$, $\gamma$, $w$) that are shared across all three studies while accommodating study-level deviations, providing a formal test of cross-context generalizability of the social generalization gradient. We also conducted pooled behavioral GLMMs spanning all three studies to formally test whether similarity-based self-anchoring and semantic generalization varied systematically across conditions, using Study 1's minimal groups as the reference category.
