Based on results available at time of writing, Sym+$\lambda$ leads model comparison and is treated as the provisional winning model pending Asym+$\lambda$ completion; if Asym+$\lambda$ wins or ties, the parameter section and figure below will be updated accordingly. As in individual studies, the two models were statistically tied in Studies 1–3, so either outcome is consistent with the symmetric architecture being sufficient to describe self-anchoring across group contexts.

**Table 6. Pooled Sym+$\lambda$ Parameter Estimates: Global and Study-Specific Means.**

| Parameter | Global | Study 1 (Minimal) | Study 2 (Status) | Study 3 (Racial) |
|:----------|-------:|------------------:|-----------------:|-----------------:|
| $\alpha$ (projection rate) | 2.02 | 2.09 | 1.83 | 2.09 |
| $\gamma$ (ingroup bias) | 0.515 | 0.401 | 0.554 | 0.580 |
| $\lambda$ (generalization) | 3.56 | 3.63 | 3.53 | 3.54 |
| $w$ (lapse rate) | 0.501 | 0.525 | 0.364 | 0.623 |

*Note.* All parameters back-transformed from probit scale: $\alpha = \Phi(\mu_{pr}) \times 10$; $\gamma = \Phi(\mu_{pr})$; $\lambda = \Phi(\mu_{pr}) \times 5$; $w = \Phi(\mu_{pr})$. Study-specific estimates are study_mu_pr posteriors, which are shrunk toward the global mean by the three-level hierarchy.

The most consistent finding is $\lambda$. The generalization sensitivity parameter estimated separately in each study — 3.57, 3.48, and 3.50 — replicated almost exactly in the pooled model (3.63, 3.53, 3.54) and converged on a global mean of 3.56. This parameter appears to reflect a stable property of how trait similarity is weighted in social generalization, independent of group type or social context.

Ingroup bias ($\gamma$) showed the clearest study-level variation. Participants in Study 1 (minimal groups) showed lower bias (pooled $\gamma$ = 0.40) than participants in Studies 2 and 3 (0.55 and 0.58, respectively). This replicates the individual study pattern and is consistent with the view that minimal group boundaries generate weaker ingroup preference than social categories carrying real-world significance. The projection rate ($\alpha$) and lapse rate ($w$) both showed hierarchical shrinkage toward the global mean relative to individual study estimates, with the most notable shift in $w$: Study 2's unusually low individual estimate (0.298) was pulled toward the global mean (0.364 in the pooled model), suggesting the extreme determinism observed in Study 2 individually was partly a sampling artifact tempered by cross-study pooling.

**Behavioral Analyses**

To formally compare self-anchoring and generalization effects across all three studies in a single model, we fit mixed-effects logistic regression models using `lme4` to the combined dataset (*N* = 507 subjects, 73,771 observations). Each study contributed its own condition levels, with Study 1's minimal-groups condition as the reference category. Predictors were Z-scored within study so that 1 unit reflects a within-study standard deviation. Random effects included study-level intercepts, subject intercepts and slopes nested within study, and crossed trait intercepts.

Across the full pooled sample, similarity-to-self was a significant predictor of ingroup classification (AME = .038, 95% CI [.021, .055], *p* < .001), as were self-evaluations (AME = .045, CI [.037, .053], *p* < .001) and desirability (AME = .036, CI [.025, .046], *p* < .001). These overall effects confirm that self-anchoring operates reliably as a cross-study phenomenon.

Condition-specific AMEs for similarity-to-self (all relative to the minimal-groups reference) revealed a striking pattern of contextual modulation. The effect was present and significant in minimal groups (AME = .053, CI [.007, .100], *p* = .025), the negation condition (AME = .053, CI [.021, .086], *p* = .001), the low-status condition (AME = .061, CI [.015, .107], *p* = .009), and the racial majority condition (AME = .033, CI [.000, .066], *p* = .050). The high-status condition showed the strongest similarity-based generalization of any condition (AME = .111, CI [.061, .162], *p* < .001) — roughly twice the size of the minimal-groups effect. The racial minority condition was the sole context with a null or directionally reversed effect (AME = −.013, CI [−.048, .021], *p* = .454), confirming the cross-study robustness of this specific boundary condition identified in Study 3.

The predicted P(ingroup) at ±1 SD of similarity-to-self further illustrates the gradient. In the high-status condition, P(ingroup) ranged from .39 at −1 SD to .62 at +1 SD (.228 range), the steepest gradient observed. Minimal groups showed a .119 range (.496 to .615), while the racial minority condition was essentially flat (.573 at −1 SD, .551 at +1 SD).

To test generalization formally — whether the similarity-based inference propagates to semantically novel traits — we fit a model with predicted.Z × Novel interactions (M4) and a three-way predicted.Z × Novel × Condition model (M5). Pooled across conditions, both trained (AME = .041, CI [.024, .059], *p* < .001) and novel-trait effects (AME = .036, CI [.019, .053], *p* < .001) were significant, confirming robust generalization at the pooled level. The three-way analysis revealed that generalization was condition-specific. In the racial minority condition, neither trained (AME = −.014, *p* = .432) nor novel-trait (AME = −.010, *p* = .580) effects were significant — a complete null. In the racial majority condition, the trained-trait effect was significant (AME = .039, CI [.005, .073], *p* = .024) but the novel-trait effect did not reach significance (AME = .025, CI [−.008, .058], *p* = .142). In contrast, all four university conditions showed significant effects for both trained and novel traits: high-status trained AME = .116 (*p* < .001), novel = .107 (*p* < .001); negation trained = .056 (*p* < .001), novel = .049 (*p* = .004); low-status trained = .064 (*p* = .007), novel = .056 (*p* = .022). Minimal groups also showed generalization to both trained (AME = .052, *p* = .033) and novel traits (AME = .056, *p* = .021).

Taken together, the pooled behavioral analyses converge with individual study findings to identify a clear principle: self-anchoring and semantic generalization are robust across minimal, university status, and racial majority contexts, but are specifically absent when the comparison involves a fellow minority group — a condition in which the shared subordinate social position may undermine the functional distinctiveness of the between-group boundary.

## GENERAL DISCUSSION
People project their attributes onto ingroup members, but the underlying cognitive mechanisms have remained largely descriptive. Using a semantic dependency network of trait relations, we formalize self-anchoring as a structured inferential process based on similarity-based generalization. Across three studies, individuals treated the self as a semantic prototype, with beliefs propagating to novel group members via relational similarity—a finding robust across minimal, university, and racial categories. Figure X shows the group-level posterior estimates for all four model parameters across all three studies, illustrating both the stability of the projection mechanism (α, λ) and the context-sensitivity of the motivational prior (γ, w) across intergroup contexts.

### Formalizing Social Identity Theory
Our research moves social identity theory from a verbal model to a formal architecture by operationalizing the metacontrast principle as a formal ratio of summed similarities. This aligns social identity research with exemplar-based models of category learning and Shepard's (1987) law of generalization. We find that self-anchoring is primarily driven by "ingroup love"—the motivation to achieve similarity with the ingroup—rather than outgroup repulsion. However, the asymmetric architecture's added value is context-dependent: the asymmetric model was marginally preferred over the symmetric model in the abstract Negation condition (where the outgroup has no concrete identity), while the symmetric model was more clearly preferred when outgroups were concrete and status-differentiated. The asymmetric architecture provided no detectable advantage in the High-Status or racial majority conditions. These dual tendencies map onto Brewer's (1991) Optimal Distinctiveness Theory, which holds that group membership satisfies simultaneous needs for assimilation (inclusion) and differentiation (distinctiveness). In the present architecture, $\alpha_{in}$ formalizes the assimilation motive and $\alpha_{out}$ formalizes the differentiation motive; the empirical question is which dominates under a given intergroup context. The symmetric architecture winning in minimal groups suggests that when neither motive has privileged content to operate on, both are absorbed into a single undifferentiated projection rate.
Prior representational claims about similarity-based inference in social categorization have been constrained by the absence of model formalism (Guest & Martin, 2021). We demonstrate that the metacontrast ratio—a central concept in social identity theory—can be precisely measured using relational similarity, and that this formalization yields testable predictions about self-anchoring that verbal accounts cannot generate. Shepard's (1987) law was derived from animal conditioning and perceptual psychophysics: organisms generalize a learned response to novel stimuli in proportion to their similarity to the training exemplar, with that gradient decaying exponentially at a rate governed by a single sensitivity parameter. Nosofsky (1986) showed the same formal structure accounts for human perceptual categorization. That an identical mathematical law appears here—where the prototype is the self, the stimuli are personality traits distributed across a semantic network, and the task is social group classification—is significant because the representational substrate is as different as possible from those original domains. The result suggests Shepard's generalization law is not perceptual or behavioral in origin but reflects a domain-general solution to a common inference problem: given what I know about one exemplar, how strongly should I predict a property of a novel one? Social identity formation, at the computational level, appears to operate via the same inference machinery Shepard identified in animal learning and Nosofsky formalized for perception—with the self functioning as a social prototype in much the same way a conditioned stimulus functions as a perceptual anchor. Both traditions emerged in parallel with Turner and Tajfel's verbal articulation of the same principles in the social domain. By extending their formal apparatus to how people generalize self-knowledge to their groups, we connect these traditions and provide an empirically tractable foundation for the representational claims Self-Categorization Theory has long advanced. A notable result within this framework is the empirical identification of $\lambda$—Shepard's generalization sensitivity—as a recoverable parameter in human social categorization data. In principle, $\lambda$ and $\alpha$ are mathematically entangled (both govern how similarity maps to categorization probability), and their joint identifiability is not guaranteed; it requires the graded semantic structure of a trait network combined with a training-to-generalization paradigm that creates distinct behavioral fingerprints for each parameter. Demonstrating that $\lambda$ is estimable from social categorization data provides a new measurement handle on self-concept breadth that cannot be reduced to projection strength, enabling researchers to formally distinguish how far the self-concept's inferential reach extends ($\lambda$) from how strongly self-beliefs are weighted in that inference ($\alpha$)—a distinction that verbal theories of self-anchoring have never been able to draw.

To close the formal loop: Turner et al. (1987) defined the metacontrast ratio verbally as the ratio of perceived intergroup difference to intragroup similarity, with categorization becoming psychologically active when this ratio is maximized. The model-derived MCR — $\text{simW}_{in} / \text{simW}_{out}$ — is the direct computational implementation of that definition, not an analogy. $\text{simW}_{in}$ and $\text{simW}_{out}$ are generalization-weighted sums of self-beliefs projected onto ingroup- versus outgroup-predictive training traits, calibrated to each participant's posterior parameter estimates. The consistent replication of MCR correlations with social identification, self-esteem, and prototypicality across all three studies validates this operationalization as capturing what Turner's verbal construct intended. The self functions here as a social prototype in the sense Rosch (1978) formalized for natural categories: the reference point relative to which group category membership is inferred.

SCT's self-as-prototype assumption predicts that participants who perceive themselves as more representative of their ingroup should show stronger social projection. Across all three studies, perceived prototypicality (Proto) did not directly predict the projection rate $\alpha$ — a null that is itself theoretically informative. $\alpha$ reflects the slope of self-to-group mapping, a process that appears to operate independently of whether participants consciously regard themselves as typical ingroup exemplars. By contrast, in Study 2, prototypicality correlated with the model-derived MCR ($r$ = .260, $p_\text{FDR}$ = .004) — the ratio of self-concept similarity signal favoring the ingroup over the outgroup. This dissociation suggests that the self-as-prototype assumption holds at the level of the *semantic contrast structure* of the self-concept (how much its organization discriminates ingroup from outgroup) rather than at the level of how steeply self-beliefs slope into ingroup classification. It is the architecture of the self-concept — not the subjective sense of representativeness — that drives differentiation.

### Self-Anchoring as Generalization Across Related Traits
Self-anchoring is an inductive reasoning process, not simple item repetition. Prior research was vulnerable to the interpretation that self-anchoring reflects repetition effects, where ratings on the same items amplify descriptiveness (Unkelbach & Rom, 2017). Demonstrating that self-evaluations generalize to novel, semantically related traits establishes that self-anchoring involves belief propagation through the trait network. Individuals do not merely infer that their group shares specific traits; they infer what their group ought to be based on the structural relations within their self-concept.

### Contextual Modulation and Social Identification
Context systematically modulates self-anchoring, though through distinct parameters across studies. In Study 2, the projection rate (α) was invariant across outgroup conditions; what changed dramatically was the prior ingroup preference (γ), which fell to near-minimal-group levels when the outgroup was a prestigious, positively-regarded rival university. This indicates that when the outgroup is desirable, participants' baseline disposition to attribute traits to the ingroup weakens—even while their similarity-weighted inference machinery operates unchanged. This pattern—invariant α, attenuated γ—was not the anticipated locus of contextual modulation; it emerged as a post-hoc observation that illuminates a distinction social identity theory has typically left implicit: the inferential process of self-anchoring and the motivational prior that activates it are separable, and only the latter appears to be contextually modulated. Behaviorally, the High-Status condition actually produced the strongest similarity-to-self effects (AME = .100), while the Low-Status condition showed attenuation (AME = .044, *p* = .082). These two patterns are not contradictory: γ is the intercept of ingroup preference, while the AME reflects the slope of similarity-based inference; a lower γ and steeper slope can co-occur if participants rely more heavily on self-information in the absence of a strong default ingroup prior. In Study 3, self-anchoring was suppressed under minority–minority contrasts, with similarity-to-self predicting ingroup classification only in the majority-outgroup condition. Self-Categorization Theory's meta-contrast principle provides a unifying account: self-anchoring functions as a categorization aid most active when the intergroup boundary is motivationally engaged but not structurally resolved. When the categorical boundary is already established through perceived status differences, self-similarity contributes little additional discriminating signal. When contrasting against a fellow minority group, both groups share a superordinate social position, which may invoke a sense of common fate that mutes the functional distinctiveness of the boundary. Positive distinctiveness motivations provide a complementary explanation: when differentiation from the outgroup is already achieved through status perceptions, self-referential inference contributes less to category definition. Together, these patterns identify self-anchoring as a context-sensitive inference strategy — deployed most actively when the categorization problem is motivationally engaged and status cues alone are insufficient to resolve it. Trait segregation analyses provide a converging signature. Across Studies 2 and 3, the condition that most suppressed self-anchoring also produced the highest trait segregation: high-status contrast in Study 2 (where γ fell sharply and behavioral AMEs were strongest) and minority-outgroup contrast in Study 3 (where AMEs were null). The direction reverses superficially — high-status produced more segregation in Study 2, minority-outgroup produced more in Study 3 — but the logic is identical in both cases: when the intergroup context removes the self-concept's organizational leverage over classification, participants impose coarser, more rigid categorical partitioning on the trait network rather than semantically structured inference. This has broader implications: the same contextual conditions that disable the assimilative inference engine — status inequality, social marginalization, outgroups that cannot be assimilated into the self-concept's semantic structure — shift group perception from graded, similarity-based categorization toward binary Us-versus-Them partitioning. The cognitive signature of trait segregation is structurally identical to what is invoked in accounts of intergroup conflict and political polarization; the present framework suggests these phenomena may share a common computational origin in the disruption of similarity-based social inference.

Within this framework, γ is the formal operationalization of SIT's positive distinctiveness motive — the baseline prior for ingroup attribution, independent of the projection mechanism. The High-Status condition in Study 2 provides the clearest empirical signature: γ fell to $M = 0.36$ when participants contrasted against a positively-regarded, higher-status outgroup — numerically identical to the group-level γ estimated in Study 1's minimal groups ($M = 0.36$). A prestigious outgroup fully erodes the ingroup preference that even a meaningless categorical assignment produces. This convergence is not coincidental: under SIT, positive distinctiveness motivation is highest when ingroup superiority is uncertain or contested. A high-status outgroup resolves the comparison unfavorably, reducing the motivational pressure to mark traits as ingroup-characteristic. The projection mechanism (α) operates unchanged; only the prior for using it shifts. Notably, γ did not similarly attenuate in Study 3's majority-outgroup condition ($M = 0.57$) — nearly matching the Negation baseline ($M = 0.60$) rather than the High-Status floor. Not all high-status outgroups are psychologically equivalent, and the γ pattern across studies reflects this. A prestigious rival university is an *aspirational* outgroup: the intergroup boundary is permeable (students could have attended UCLA instead of UCR), the outgroup is positively regarded, and no historical power asymmetry structures the comparison. Under these conditions, positive distinctiveness is already contested — the outgroup is objectively superior on the relevant status dimension — reducing the motivational need to mark traits as ingroup-characteristic. A dominant racial majority is a *marginalized* outgroup comparison: the boundary is relatively impermeable, the power asymmetry is entrenched, and minority identity is bound up with protection against that asymmetry. Facing the racial majority activates a defensive ingroup prior — sustaining γ near baseline levels ($M = 0.57$) despite the status differential — because positive distinctiveness under these conditions requires active maintenance rather than passive erosion. In Study 3, the lapse rate $w$ — rather than γ — was the contextually sensitive parameter, rising in the minority-outgroup condition ($M = 0.64$) relative to the majority condition ($M = 0.56$) and relative to both Studies 1 and 2 ($M \approx 0.56$). This cross-study pattern in $w$ is substantive, not artifactual: Studies 1 and 2 produced equivalent lapse rates despite differing in group content richness (arbitrary minimal groups vs. real universities), while Study 3's racial context elevated noise. This is consistent with van Veelen et al.'s (2017) account that self-anchoring is most tractable when group content is uncertain — racial categories carry pre-loaded stereotypic content that competes with self-based inference, increasing classification stochasticity without suppressing the self-anchoring mechanism entirely (as confirmed by the replication of MCR–personality correlations across all three studies).

Including the generalization sensitivity parameter, λ, operationalizes the decay of self-anchoring across the semantic network and functions as a person-specific index of cognitive style. High λ indicates a steep, narrow generalization gradient, where inference is restricted to only the most semantically proximal traits; low λ indicates a shallow, broad gradient where self-knowledge propagates more liberally. The finding that higher social identification correlated with higher λ in Study 2 (*r* = .25) is informative. It suggests that stronger group identification does not produce a more expansive or all-encompassing ingroup category; instead, it sharpens the inferential boundary. Strongly identified individuals appear to use a more selective, high-fidelity mapping from self to group, anchoring primarily on their most diagnostic attributes. This provides a formal, mechanistic account for how group attachment shapes the *structure*, not just the magnitude, of social inference.

### Limitations
Although $\lambda$ enables formal estimation of the asymmetric model with separate $\alpha_{in}$ and $\alpha_{out}$ parameters, the binary forced-choice paradigm imposes a structural constraint on the behavioral leverage available to dissociate these quantities. Because each trial yields a single ingroup-or-outgroup response, ingroup attractiveness and outgroup repulsion cannot vary independently within a trial—both are absorbed into the same binary outcome, limiting the data's informativeness for pulling the two projection rates apart. This means that even in contexts where $\alpha_{in}$ and $\alpha_{out}$ genuinely differ, the forced-choice design may be insufficiently sensitive to detect the asymmetry. Paradigms that solicit independent ingroup and outgroup typicality ratings, or that present single-group classification trials, would provide richer behavioral signatures for estimating these parameters separately. The consistent symmetric-architecture preference across most intergroup contexts should therefore be interpreted cautiously: it may partly reflect task design constraints rather than a genuine cognitive indistinguishability of ingroup love and outgroup hate. Future work with paradigms better suited to generating independent behavioral signatures for $\alpha_{in}$ and $\alpha_{out}$ would provide a stronger test of whether the symmetric constraint is empirically warranted. The trait pool used across all three studies consisted entirely of positively valenced traits. This is a meaningful constraint on interpretation of the ingroup bias parameter ($\gamma$). Because all traits are desirable, a $\gamma$ above 0.5 — indicating preferential classification of trait-bearers as ingroup members — is consistent with positive ingroup distinctiveness: participants attribute valued characteristics to their group at above-chance rates. The higher $\gamma$ observed in real social category contexts (Studies 2 and 3, $\gamma \approx$ 0.55–0.59) relative to minimal groups (Study 1, $\gamma \approx$ 0.36–0.40) is interpretable as heightened positive ingroup bias when group boundaries carry social meaning. However, because the design includes no negatively valenced traits, the model cannot separately estimate whether participants are attributing positive traits to the ingroup, withholding positive traits from the outgroup, or both. Outgroup derogation via negative trait assignment — a distinct component of intergroup bias — is entirely outside the paradigm's scope. Future work incorporating both positive and negative traits would allow $\gamma$ to reflect the full valence structure of ingroup favoritism and outgroup derogation independently. Of SCT's four fit criteria, neither normative fit nor perceiver readiness is directly assessed. Normative fit — whether trait content matches expectations for a group label — is not measured; the task does not ask participants to evaluate content-label consistency. Perceiver readiness is imposed by the task structure: all participants classify traits for an experimentally salient group, so the model describes how self-anchoring operates once a category is engaged, not who spontaneously activates social categorization in naturalistic settings. Comparative fit was explored via λ variation across Study 2 conditions, but effects were small (R² = .039) and the mapping from λ to categorical distinctiveness is indirect — these analyses should be understood as exploratory rather than as formal tests of comparative fit.

### Conclusion
By formalizing the relationship between self-concept structure and social identity, we show that self-anchoring follows the same principles of similarity-based generalization that govern category learning—at least across the intergroup contexts examined here, all drawn from university samples. Group membership is not merely a motivational bias; it is a structured, inferential process grounded in semantic self-knowledge. In this sense, the self-concept functions as a generative engine of social identity: beliefs about social groups are not stored as fixed templates but constructed on-the-fly by propagating self-knowledge through relational semantic structure—the same inferential machinery used for any categorical judgment. This generative architecture explains both the robustness of self-anchoring across heterogeneous group contexts and its vulnerability to disruption when the intergroup structure renders the self-concept's semantic geometry an unreliable guide. This architecture provides a precise, testable framework for understanding social identity as a cognitive process.

### Appendix A: Posterior Predictive Checks
We conducted posterior predictive checks (PPCs) to verify model fit to observed data, evaluating both the training and generalization phases across all three studies (Figure A1). Observed and predicted data were well-aligned, confirming adequate fit.

### Appendix B: Parameter Recovery Analyses
We assessed parameter identifiability by simulating behavior from known true parameters, then fitting the model to the simulated data and comparing recovered posteriors to ground truth. The simulation used the Study 1 trial structure (*N* = 61), real trait similarity matrices, and two design choices described below.

**Parameter generation.** True parameters for each simulated participant were drawn from distributions calibrated to the Study 1 posterior rather than from the prior. Group-level means ($\mu_{pr}$) and individual-level standard deviations ($\sigma$) on the probit scale were taken directly from the Study 1 posterior summaries for each model (Sym+$\lambda$: $\sigma_m = 0.286$, $\sigma_\gamma = 0.709$, $\sigma_\lambda = 0.334$, $\sigma_w = 1.181$; Asym+$\lambda$: $\sigma_{\alpha_{in}} = 0.220$, $\sigma_{\alpha_{out}} = 0.226$, $\sigma_\gamma = 0.721$, $\sigma_\lambda = 0.377$, $\sigma_w = 1.188$). This ensures simulated individual differences match the range actually observed in the data rather than an arbitrary prior specification.

**Self-rating generation.** Each simulated participant received synthetic self-ratings drawn from a Gaussian Markov Random Field (GMRF) defined on the trait network. We computed the precision matrix $\mathbf{P} = \alpha\mathbf{L} + \varepsilon\mathbf{I}_{148}$, where $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$ is the combinatorial graph Laplacian of the trait network, $\alpha = 1.0$ controls network smoothness, and $\varepsilon = 0.01$ regularizes the singular Laplacian. Each participant received an independent draw $\mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\, \mathbf{P}^{-1})$, standardized to the observed within-person SD (1.13), centered at 4, and rounded to integers 1–7. Intuitively, the graph Laplacian encodes which traits are structurally proximate in the network; inverting the regularized Laplacian produces a covariance matrix in which connected traits covary — a participant who rates *Warm* highly will tend to rate *Friendly* similarly, exactly the structure the projection model assumes. Centering ratings at the scale midpoint (4) ensures that self-ratings span both the self-descriptive and non-self-descriptive range, which is required for $m$ to be identifiable from the data.

Primary parameters of interest — projection rate ($m$ / $\alpha_{in}$, $\alpha_{out}$), ingroup bias ($\gamma$), generalization sensitivity ($\lambda$), and lapse rate ($w$) — were recoverable for both the Symmetric+$\lambda$ and Asymmetric+$\lambda$ architectures (Figure B1). [PENDING — insert per-parameter recovery correlations (*r*) and RMSE after `Parameter Recovery/run_parameter_recovery.R` completes.] Figure B2 shows the parameter confusion matrix: each cell gives the Pearson *r* between true parameter *i* and recovered parameter *j*, with diagonal cells (outlined) reflecting self-recovery and off-diagonal cells reflecting cross-parameter confusability.

### Supplementary Materials C: Race Moderation Analyses (Study 3)

Study 3 pools Asian and Latino participants within each contrast condition, an assumption that warrants direct examination. We tested whether participant race (Asian vs. Latino) moderated the condition effects reported in the main text by adding a condition × race interaction term to each parameter model.

**Parameter estimates by condition × race.** Cell means for key parameters are shown in Table C1.

| Condition | Race | $\gamma$ | $\lambda$ | $w$ | MCR |
|:---|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Minority | Asian | 0.69 | 3.49 | 0.65 | 4.62 |
| Minority | Latino | 0.41 | 3.49 | 0.64 | 7.42 |
| Majority | Asian | 0.63 | 3.49 | 0.60 | 6.78 |
| Majority | Latino | 0.50 | 3.50 | 0.52 | 6.12 |

*Note.* N(Asian) = 130, N(Latino) = 135; Minority: Asian N=59, Latino N=79; Majority: Asian N=71, Latino N=56.

**Condition × race interaction.** A significant condition × race interaction emerged for $\gamma$ (F(1, 261) = 6.53, *p* = .011). Within the Minority condition, Asian participants showed substantially higher ingroup classification bias ($M$ = 0.69) than Latino participants ($M$ = 0.41). This asymmetry arises because within the Minority (Asian-vs-Latino) contrast, Asians and Latinos occupy opposite ingroup/outgroup roles: an Asian participant's ingroup is Asian, while a Latino participant's ingroup is Latino. The apparent "low bias" for Latinos in the Minority condition may reflect that Latinos in the sample were less activated by the intergroup contrast, or that within-minority contrasts have different salience by racial group. A Latino participant's condition effect (Minority $M$ = 0.41 vs. Majority $M$ = 0.50, *p* = .032) shows higher bias against the racial majority than against a fellow minority, whereas Asian participants showed no significant condition difference (*p* = .149). The lapse rate condition effect was driven entirely by Latino participants (within-Latino: Minority $M$ = 0.64 vs. Majority $M$ = 0.52, *p* = .021; within-Asian: *p* = .360). No condition × race interactions were significant for $\alpha$ (F = 0.17, *p* = .679), $\lambda$ (F = 0.32, *p* = .571), or $\Delta$ELPD (F = 0.72, *p* = .399). The MCR × condition × race interaction was marginal (F(1, 261) = 3.30, *p* = .070).

**MCR–personality correlations by race.** MCR correlated with independent self-construal (SING.Ind) and self-esteem (RSE) in both Asian and Latino participants (all *p*s ≤ .021), confirming the core MCR-personality structure across both groups. Self-prototypicality (Proto) correlated with MCR in Latino participants (*r* = .227, *p* = .009) but not Asian participants (*r* = −.028, *p* = .753; Fisher *z* = −2.06, *p* = .039), suggesting that the Proto → MCR pathway observed in Study 2 replicates for Latinos but not Asians. Social identification (SI) correlated with MCR in Asian participants (*r* = .225, *p* = .011) but not Latinos (*r* = .093, *p* = .289; *p*~diff~ = .225). These race-stratified patterns should be interpreted cautiously given sample sizes within each race × condition cell (N = 56–79).

**Warmth moderation by race.** A marginal race × ingroup-over-minority preference interaction for MCR (F(1, 230) = 3.14, *p* = .078) suggested opposite directions for Asian (*β* = −.059) and Latino (*β* = +.034) participants, though neither within-race slope was significant. No other warmth × race interactions reached significance. All race moderation results are exploratory, were not pre-registered, and should be replicated before interpretation.

### Supplementary Materials D: Self-Concept Entropy (*H_g*) and Ingroup Classification

We computed a *local self-concept clarity* index (*H_g*) as a similarity-weighted Shannon entropy over the self-evaluation distribution in each test trait's semantic neighborhood:

$$H_g = -\sum_{e=1}^{7} p_e \log_2 p_e, \quad p_e = \frac{\sum_{t:\, E_t = e} S_{tg}}{\sum_{t=1}^{T} S_{tg}}$$

where $p_e$ is the similarity-weighted proportion of training traits rated at level $e$ on the 7-point scale. Low $H_g$ indicates coherent, concentrated self-ratings near the test trait; high $H_g$ indicates mixed, diffuse self-ratings. This operationalizes Campbell et al.'s (1996) self-concept clarity at the local semantic level. Each study used a separate mixed-effects logistic regression with desirability controlled and a by-subject random slope for $H_g$.

$H_g$ was non-significant in Study 1 (AME = −.058, 95% CI [−.152, .036], *p* = .225), consistent with low statistical power and the high lapse rate under minimal-group conditions. $H_g$ significantly predicted lower ingroup classification in Study 2 (AME = −.058, 95% CI [−.099, −.017], *p* = .005) and Study 3 (AME = −.051, 95% CI [−.096, −.006], *p* = .027). These results are consistent with a signal-precision account: when group content is real and self-anchoring is the primary inferential channel, a diffuse local self-concept degrades classification. The null in Study 1 is consistent with the high lapse rate (*w* = 0.56) under minimal-group conditions attenuating behavioral leverage for detecting entropy effects.

### Supplementary Materials E: Canonical Correlation Analysis

**Study 1 CCA (Minimal Groups, *N* = 61).** To examine the multivariate personality structure of model-derived indices, we conducted an exploratory CCA of model parameters (X: $\alpha$, $\lambda$, $\gamma$, $w$, MCR, trait segregation; $k = 6$) against personality scales (Y: DS, Prototypicality, SCC, Social Identity, RSE, NTB, NFC, SING-Ind, SING-Inter; $k = 9$). Statistical significance was assessed via permutation test (*B* = 5,000). *N* = 61 falls below recommended guidelines for CCA with 15 variables; results should be regarded as preliminary and interpreted with caution. The first canonical variate was significant (*r* = .720, *p*~perm~ = .013). On the model side, CV1 was defined primarily by MCR (loading = .53), ingroup bias $\gamma$ (loading = .45), and trait segregation (loading = .39); $\alpha$, $\lambda$, and $w$ loaded negligibly. On the personality side, SING-Inter dominated (loading = .87), followed by social identity (loading = .53) and need to belong (loading = .48). A second variate was also significant (*r* = .623, *p*~perm~ = .005) but is not interpreted given the sample size. The pooled CCA below provides better-powered replication.

**Pooled CCA (*N* = 507).** *[Pending — pooled individual-difference parameters are being finalized. Results will be inserted here prior to submission.]*

### Supplementary Materials F: Semantic Trait Network

The semantic dependency network used in all three studies comprised 148 personality traits. Figure F1 displays a force-directed layout of the 80 most-connected traits (Fruchterman–Reingold algorithm). Node size and color reflect degree centrality. Traits with high connectivity occupy the network's densely interconnected core and have broad semantic influence during the similarity-weighted inference process; low-degree traits at the periphery exert narrower inferential reach and primarily receive rather than propagate generalization weight.

```{r}
#| label: fig-f1-trait-network
#| fig-cap: "Semantic trait network (top 80 traits by connectivity). Nodes represent personality traits; edges represent adjacency in the semantic dependency network. Node size and color indicate degree centrality (number of connections). Force-directed layout (Fruchterman–Reingold). Trait labels omitted for clarity; the full adjacency matrix is available in the Open Materials."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7
#| eval: !expr file.exists(fig_path("fig01_trait_network.tiff"))
```

## OPEN MATERIALS

Analysis scripts, Stan model code, and de-identified data are available at [repository URL]. An interactive web supplement demonstrating the Symmetric + λ and Asymmetric + λ model architectures is available at [Shiny app URL]. The supplement allows readers to manipulate model parameters and resample training-trait configurations in real time. Two parameter combinations are particularly informative as reference points: setting γ = 0.50 and w = 0 isolates the core self-anchoring mechanism — no baseline ingroup preference and no random responding — so that the classification curve reflects only the similarity-weighted self-concept signal. The Study 1 group-level posterior medians (γ = 0.36, w = 0.56) are loaded by default, reflecting the modest ingroup bias and substantial response noise typical of laboratory categorization paradigms.
